questions.stem: Cortisol binds an intracellular receptor that acts as a transcription factor. Which other messenger uses the same receptor superfamily?
questions.explanation: Lipophilic messengers (steroids, thyroid hormone, retinoic acid, vitamin D) cross the membrane and bind the steroid/thyroid hormone receptor superfamily. A: Catecholamines are polar and bind surface receptors. C: Insulin is a polypeptide acting on a surface receptor tyrosine kinase. D: Cytokines are proteins that use surface receptors. E: Acetylcholine acts on surface ion channel (nicotinic) receptors.

questions.stem: Endothelial cells release prostacyclin, which relaxes the adjacent vascular smooth muscle. This is an example of which signaling mode?
questions.explanation: PGI2 from endothelial cells acts on nearby cells of a different type (smooth muscle): paracrine. A: Endocrine signals travel in the blood to distant cells. B: Autocrine acts on the secreting cell or cells of the same type. C: Gap junctions pass small molecules such as Ca²⁺ directly between cells. D: Direct signaling through surface receptors needs cell-to-cell contact, as in the immune system.

questions.stem: Compared with aspirin, a glucocorticoid reduces synthesis of a broader range of eicosanoids, including leukotrienes. Why?

options.B: It inhibits phospholipase C, blocking IP3 and DAG
options.C: It blocks prostaglandin receptors on target cells
options.D: It inhibits phospholipase A2, so arachidonic acid isn't released
options.E: It inhibits adenylyl cyclase in injured cells

questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids inhibit PLA2, which releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, so the whole eicosanoid cascade shuts down; aspirin and NSAIDs inhibit only downstream COX. A: Irreversible COX inhibition is aspirin's action, which spares leukotrienes. B: PLC makes IP3 and DAG, not arachidonate. C: Receptor blockade wouldn't reduce synthesis. E: Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, not eicosanoids.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman has leg weakness that worsens with walking and recovers with rest, slurred speech after long phone calls, and ptosis by evening. What is the mechanism of her disease?

options.A: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
options.C: Blockade of ACh release by a bacterial toxin

questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis: anti-AChR antibodies cross-link receptors, which are endocytosed and degraded, giving fatigable weakness. A: Lambert–Eaton (improves with use). B: Loss of AChE would increase ACh effect. C: Botulism (descending paralysis, not fatigable pattern). D: Demyelination gives a different pattern (e.g., Guillain–Barré).

questions.stem: Cortisol enters a cell and binds the glucocorticoid receptor in the cytoplasm. What happens next?

options.A: The receptor autophosphorylates and recruits Grb2
options.B: The receptor activates Gs, raising cAMP
options.C: The receptor opens an ion channel in the membrane
options.D: Heat shock proteins dissociate, exposing an NLS
options.E: The receptor binds its response element in the cytoplasm

questions.explanation: Cortisol binding changes the receptor's conformation: it releases its heat shock proteins, exposing a nuclear localization signal, then dimerizes and moves to the nucleus to bind the hormone-response element. A: Autophosphorylation and Grb2 are RTK signaling. B: Gs and cAMP are GPCR signaling. C: Ion channel receptors are surface receptors for neurotransmitters. E: The hormone-response element is DNA, in the nucleus.

questions.stem: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of nicotinic ACh receptors. Why does pyridostigmine improve muscle strength?

options.A: It stimulates synthesis of new receptors
options.B: More ACh reaches the remaining receptors
options.C: It blocks binding of anti-receptor antibodies
options.E: It acts directly as a nicotinic agonist

questions.explanation: Pyridostigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: ACh accumulates in the cleft, so the fewer remaining receptors are occupied more often. It is symptomatic, so immunosuppressants are added. A: It doesn't increase receptor synthesis. C: Antibody production is reduced by immunosuppressants, not by AChE inhibitors. D: Pyridostigmine is reversible; irreversible AChE inhibitors are nerve agents. E: It acts on the enzyme, not on the receptor.
